title: Is customizing a CRM considered R&D for tax purposes?
description: Customizing a CRM can qualify for the federal R&D credit under IRC § 41 only when custom components resolve technological uncertainty.
summary: Customizing a CRM system can qualify for the U.S. federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41 only when specific custom components resolve genuine technological uncertainty through documented experimentation. Routine configuration of off-the-shelf platforms does not qualify, back-office internal use software must meet a high threshold of innovation test, and customer-facing functionality avoids that hurdle entirely.

body.text: Customizing a CRM system can qualify for the U.S. federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41 only when specific custom components resolve genuine technological uncertainty through documented experimentation. Routine configuration of off-the-shelf platforms does not qualify, back-office internal use software must meet a high threshold of innovation test, and customer-facing functionality avoids that hurdle entirely.
Jurisdiction: United States of America. This is general information, not tax or legal advice.
1. Short answer

Customizing a customer relationship management (CRM) system is not research and development for U.S. federal tax purposes merely because it involves software work. Under the credit for increasing research activities in Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) §41, only the portion of a CRM project that sets out to eliminate a genuine technological uncertainty about capability, method or appropriate design, through a process of experimentation that fundamentally relies on computer science or engineering principles, can qualify. Routine configuration of a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) CRM platform does not.

Three additional U.S. rules shape the answer for CRM work specifically. First, back-office CRM functionality that is developed for use in general and administrative functions is internal use software (IUS) under I.R.C. §41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6), and it must clear an additional three-part "high threshold of innovation" test. Second, CRM functionality developed to enable the taxpayer to interact with third parties, or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system (for example, a customer self-service portal), is by regulation not internal use software at all. Third, CRM software that serves both purposes is "dual function software," which the regulations presume to be internal use software unless the taxpayer can isolate a third-party subset or qualifies for a 25 percent safe harbor.

Separately from the credit, amounts paid or incurred in connection with the development of software, including qualifying CRM development, are treated as research or experimental expenditures under I.R.C. §174A, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) added for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. Treatment as a §174A expenditure is a precondition to, not a substitute for, meeting the §41 qualified research tests.
2. The frameworks that decide the question
2.1 United States: I.R.C. §41 "qualified research"

Section 41(d)(1) defines qualified research as research (A) with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A; (B) which is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature and the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer; and (C) substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in §41(d)(3). Under §41(d)(3)(A), research is conducted for a permitted purpose if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality. Under §41(d)(3)(B), research is in no event treated as conducted for a permitted purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors.

A "business component" under §41(d)(2)(B) is any product, process, computer software, technique, formula or invention that is held for sale, lease or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. For CRM projects, the business component is usually defined at the level of a specific piece of software, such as a custom integration module, a custom data-synchronization service, or a custom scoring engine, rather than the CRM platform as a whole.

Currency note: For tax years beginning in 2022 through 2024, the cross-reference was to specified research or experimental expenditures under §174 as amended by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act; for earlier years, it was to expenses that may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under §174. Readers should confirm which version applies to the tax year being claimed.

Software development under §174A: Section 174A(d)(3) treats any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software as a research or experimental expenditure. For a CRM project, this means the development portion of qualifying custom code is a §174A expenditure that, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, may be deducted currently or, at the taxpayer's election, capitalized and amortized. Eligible small business taxpayers (those meeting the gross receipts test of §448(c)) may elect to apply §174A retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, under procedures in Rev. Proc. 2025-28. Treatment as a §174A expenditure does not, by itself, make CRM work qualified research for credit purposes; the remaining §41 tests and exclusions must still be met.
2.2 Comparative context: Australia's R&D Tax Incentive (R&DTI)
It describes Australian law and does not affect the U.S. analysis.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) and the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR) jointly administer the R&DTI. R&D activities must be registered with DISR before the offset is claimed through the tax return, and a registration number does not by itself confirm that the activities are eligible. To get a tax offset, R&D expenditure for the income year must be at least A$20,000. According to the business.gov.au eligibility page, that threshold does not apply where a research service provider conducts the R&D, or where the entity contributes to the Cooperative Research Centres Program.

The ATO page describing the program does not use the phrase "most significant lever." It describes the incentive's aims as boosting competitiveness and improving productivity across the Australian economy and encouraging R&D that might not otherwise be conducted. U.S. readers should note that there is no U.S. analog to the Australian minimum expenditure threshold or pre-registration requirement; the U.S. credit is claimed on Form 6765 with the return or on an amended return, subject to the reporting requirements discussed in Section 7.
2.3 A note on the Frascati Manual

The OECD's Frascati Manual 2015 sets out five core criteria, all of which must be met for an activity to be counted as R&D for statistical purposes: the activity must be novel, creative, uncertain, systematic, and transferable and/or reproducible. More importantly for U.S. taxpayers, the Frascati Manual is a statistical measurement standard and is not U.S. tax law. The governing U.S. test is the statutory test in I.R.C. §41(d), as interpreted by Treas. Reg. §1.41-4 and the federal courts. The IRS does not apply the Frascati criteria when examining a §41 claim, and a CRM project that satisfies the Frascati criteria could still fail §41 (for example, under the internal use software rules or the substantially-all requirement).
3. The decisive question: was there a technological uncertainty?
3.1 How uncertainty is defined

United States. Under Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1), uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product. The same regulation provides that whether expenditures qualify as research or experimental expenditures depends on the nature of the activity to which the expenditures relate, not on the nature of the product or improvement being developed or the level of technological advancement the product or improvement represents, and that the ultimate success, failure, sale or use of the product is not relevant. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) likewise provides that a taxpayer need not succeed in developing a new or improved business component to satisfy the discovery requirement. For CRM work, a failed attempt to build a custom synchronization layer that was abandoned in favor of a different architecture can still be qualified research if the other tests are met.

Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) also provides that the discovery requirement does not require the taxpayer to seek information that exceeds, expands or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor to obtain a patent. A CRM team need not invent something new to the software industry; it must, however, face uncertainty that the information available to it at the outset did not resolve.

The "competent professional" standard. It comes from the United Kingdom's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) Guidelines on the Meaning of Research and Development for Tax Purposes. Paragraph 13 of those guidelines describes scientific or technological uncertainty as existing when knowledge of whether something is possible or feasible, or how to achieve it in practice, is not readily available or deducible by a competent professional working in the field, and paragraph 14 adds that uncertainties a competent professional can readily resolve are not scientific or technological uncertainties. Those guidelines apply to UK accounting periods beginning on or after April 1, 2023. The U.S. test, by contrast, asks what information is available to the taxpayer (Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1)). In practice, U.S. examiners look at whether vendor documentation, published API specifications, certified connectors, or standard industry practice already established how to achieve the CRM result; if so, uncertainty about capability, method or design is unlikely to exist.
3.2 Integration uncertainty, the usual route for CRM work

Uncertainty about the "appropriate design" of a business component under Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1) can arise when the taxpayer knows the desired result and the individual tools but does not know how to combine them within real constraints, such as data volumes, transaction throughput, latency limits imposed by a legacy order system, or API call limits imposed by the CRM vendor. The UK guidelines recognize a parallel concept: paragraph 29 refers to "system uncertainty" arising from the complexity of a system rather than from how its individual components behave, and paragraph 30 indicates that uncertainty can exist where it is not readily deducible how separate components should be combined to achieve the intended function, even when the principles of integration are well known.
The underlying principle stands, and in the U.S. it is expressed through the "appropriate design" limb of Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1).

The shrinking-back rule. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2) provides that the qualified research tests are applied first at the level of the discrete business component. If the component as a whole does not satisfy the tests, they are then applied to the most significant subset of elements of the component, and so on, "shrinking back" until a subset is reached that satisfies the requirements or the most basic element is reached. For CRM projects, this rule is central: a company-wide CRM rollout will rarely satisfy the substantially-all test as a whole, but a discrete custom integration service within it may.
4. The U.S. four-part test applied to CRM customization

headers: What it means for CRM customization (analysis)

cells: Section 174A / permitted purpose

§41(d)(1)(A) and §41(d)(3): expenditures must be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under §174A (for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024), and the research must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality. Style, taste, cosmetic and seasonal design factors are excluded under §41(d)(3)(B).

Changing page layouts, colors, field labels or dashboard arrangements in a CRM is cosmetic or routine and excluded. Work aimed at measurable gains in function or performance, such as the throughput, latency or reliability of a custom integration, can serve a permitted purpose.
Technological in nature

Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(4): information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. A taxpayer may use existing technologies and may rely on existing principles.

CRM work rooted in computer science (data architecture, concurrency control, distributed synchronization, algorithms) can meet this test. Sales-process redesign, business-rule mapping or user-experience preference testing does not.
Elimination of uncertainty
§41(d)(1)(B); Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1): uncertainty about capability, method or appropriate design of the business component.

The question is whether the team knew at the outset how to achieve the result within the platform's constraints. Documented API behavior, certified connectors or vendor guidance usually removes uncertainty.
Process of experimentation

§41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(5)(i): a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset. It involves identifying the uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate it, and conducting a process of evaluating the alternatives (for example, modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error). Under §1.41-4(a)(6), "substantially all" means 80 percent or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, applied separately to each business component.
Evidence should show the alternatives considered, the tests run, and the results, including failures, for the specific CRM component being claimed.

body.text: The statute confirms that research toward an improved business component can qualify (§41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and (d)(3)(A)), and Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1) provides that eligibility does not depend on the level of technological advancement the improvement represents. The specific "small or incremental" characterization, however, comes from commentary and is not stated in those words in the statute or regulations reviewed.
4.1 Statutory exclusions that commonly reach CRM work
Even where the four-part test appears to be met, I.R.C. §41(d)(4) lists activities that are never qualified research. Several apply directly to CRM customization:

items: Research after commercial production (§41(d)(4)(A)). Activities conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component are excluded. For software, ongoing maintenance, bug fixing and routine updates after a CRM customization has been deployed for its intended use generally fall here.

Adaptation of existing business components (§41(d)(4)(B)). Research related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need is excluded. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(10), Example 3, concludes that activities adapting an existing software program to a particular customer's requirement or need are excluded from qualified research. A consultant that configures an existing CRM product for a client, or a vendor that tailors its own existing CRM module for one customer, faces this exclusion unless the work goes beyond adaptation and involves a genuine process of experimentation.

Duplication of existing business components (§41(d)(4)(C)). Reproducing an existing business component, in whole or in part, from a physical examination of the component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications or publicly available information is excluded. Rebuilding functionality that the CRM vendor or another product already provides, from published specifications, is not qualified research.

Surveys, studies and similar activities (§41(d)(4)(D)). Efficiency surveys, management function or technique activities, market research and routine data collection are excluded. Business process reengineering that accompanies a CRM implementation falls here.

Funded research (§41(d)(4)(H)). Research to the extent funded by any grant, contract or otherwise by another person is excluded. A CRM implementation partner whose payment is not contingent on success, or which does not retain substantial rights in the results, generally cannot claim the credit for that work; the client may be the party entitled to claim it, subject to the contract-research rules in §41(b)(3).

body.text: 4.2 Worked example: the 80 percent "substantially all" test (hypothetical)

Hypothetical. A company builds a custom middleware layer to synchronize a cloud CRM with a legacy order database. Its time records attribute 1,250 hours of research activity to the middleware business component. Of these, 1,040 hours are documented as identifying the uncertainty, designing alternative synchronization approaches and testing them.

items: Step 1: Share of activities that are elements of a process of experimentation = 1,040 ÷ 1,250 = 0.832.
Step 3: 83.2 percent is at least 80 percent, so the substantially-all requirement in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6) is met for this component, provided the hours are substantiated.

Contrast: if only 960 of the 1,250 hours were documented as experimentation, the share would be 960 ÷ 1,250 = 0.768 = 76.8 percent, below the 80 percent threshold. Under the shrinking-back rule in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2), the taxpayer could then test the most significant subset of the middleware (for example, the conflict-resolution engine alone) to see whether that subset satisfies the requirement.

body.text: Note that §1.41-4(a)(6) permits measurement on a cost basis or another consistently applied reasonable basis; hours are used here only for illustration. The Seventh Circuit's decision in Little Sandy Coal (Section 7.1) emphasizes that reconstructed or shortcut estimates of experimentation time are unlikely to carry the burden of proof.
5. The internal use software hurdle
5.1 Is a CRM "internal use software"?

Section 41(d)(4)(E) excludes, except to the extent provided in regulations, research with respect to computer software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer, other than for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research or in a production process that meets the §41(d)(1) requirements. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6)(iii), software is developed primarily for internal use if it is developed for use in general and administrative functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business. The regulations limit general and administrative functions to financial management functions, human resource management functions, and support services functions. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6)(iv), software is not developed primarily for internal use if it is developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed or otherwise marketed to third parties, or if it is developed to enable the taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system.

These rules were adopted in T.D. 9786 (final regulations published in October 2016). Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(e), paragraph (c)(6) applies to taxable years beginning on or after October 4, 2016; for taxable years ending on or after January 20, 2015, and beginning before October 4, 2016, the IRS will not challenge return positions consistent with all of paragraph (c)(6).

Under the regulation, CRM functionality that lets customers or other third parties interact with the taxpayer's system (for example, a customer portal that lets customers open service cases, track orders or review account data) falls outside internal use software. Back-office CRM functionality used only to support general and administrative functions (for example, internal commission calculations feeding financial management, or internal reporting used only by support services) is the part exposed to the higher standard.
5.2 Dual function CRM software

Many CRM customizations serve both purposes at once: the same data layer supports internal sales administration and an external customer portal. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6)(vi) addresses this "dual function software." Under §1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A), dual function software is presumed to be developed primarily for the taxpayer's internal use. Under §1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B), the presumption does not apply to the extent the taxpayer can identify a subset of elements of the dual function software that only enables the taxpayer to interact with third parties or allows third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system (a "third-party subset"). Under the safe harbor in §1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C), if the taxpayer cannot identify such a subset, or for the remaining dual function subset, the taxpayer may include 25 percent of the qualified research expenditures of the dual function software (or subset) in computing the credit, provided the taxpayer's third-party use is reasonably anticipated to constitute at least 10 percent of the software's use, measured using an objective, reasonable method within the taxpayer's industry.

Hypothetical illustration. A company incurs $400,000 of qualified research expenditures developing a custom CRM case-management engine used both by internal support staff and, through a portal, by customers. It cannot isolate a third-party subset, but it reasonably anticipates that customer-initiated transactions will make up at least 10 percent of the engine's use under an objective industry measure. Under the safe harbor, it may include 25 percent × $400,000 = $100,000 of those expenditures without satisfying the high threshold of innovation test, assuming the four-part test is otherwise met. To claim more, it would need either to identify a third-party subset or to show that the engine satisfies the high threshold of innovation test.
5.3 The high threshold of innovation test
Internal use software must satisfy the §41 requirements and the high threshold of innovation test in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). It has three conditions, all of which must be met:

cells: Innovative

The software would result in a reduction in cost, improvement in speed, or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful. The standard is objective and does not turn on how unique or novel the software is.
Significant economic risk

The taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development, and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period. The regulation states that this standard requires a higher level of uncertainty and technical risk than is required for software that is not internal use software. Technical risk arises from uncertainty about capability or methodology that exists at the beginning of the development.
Not commercially available
The software cannot be purchased, leased or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the innovative and significant economic risk requirements.

body.text: 6. Routine configuration versus qualifying development
The classifications below apply the U.S. tests above; individual examples drawn from commentary are labeled as such.

cells: Objective

Fitting existing platform features to business requirements, or cosmetic changes (excluded under §41(d)(3)(B)); adapting an existing component to a particular customer's need (excluded under §41(d)(4)(B)).
Resolving uncertainty about capability, method or appropriate design (Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1)) for a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality.
Uncertainty
Solution available from vendor documentation, documented APIs, certified connectors or standard practice.

How to achieve the result within the platform's limits or across systems is not known at the outset (appropriate design uncertainty; compare the UK "system uncertainty" concept in DSIT guidelines paragraphs 29–30).
Typical examples
Adding custom fields, configuring dashboards, workflows and permissions, installing certified connectors, standard data migration, mapping sales processes, post-deployment maintenance (§41(d)(4)(A)).
Custom integration code where standard connectors fail to meet performance or reliability requirements; new algorithms or models beyond native capability.
Internal use status
Back-office administrative customizations are internal use software and face the high threshold of innovation test.
Customer- or partner-facing functionality is not internal use software (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)); dual function software may use a third-party subset or the 25 percent safe harbor.
Evidence
Implementation plans, setup checklists, user guides.
Contemporaneous records of the uncertainty identified, alternatives considered, tests and results (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(5)(i)), organized by business component to support Form 6765 Section G.

body.text: Building on established cryptographic libraries and published protocols would ordinarily not involve uncertainty under Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1); designing a novel scheme to meet a specific performance or compliance constraint might, depending on the facts.
6.1 Comparative context: Australia's software exclusion and supporting activities

DISR's guide Software-related activities and R&D Tax Incentive (May 2024) indicates that developing, modifying or customizing software for the dominant purpose of internal business administration (with examples such as payroll, accounting, invoicing, ordering and quality control reports) falls within the Australian software exclusion, and that customizing an off-the-shelf package can be covered depending on the software's dominant purpose. Supporting R&D activities must be undertaken for the dominant purpose of supporting a core R&D activity; the guide's example is customizing software on a production line to facilitate an experiment in an eligible core R&D activity, with only the portion used for experiments claimable. The U.S. analog is narrower in some respects and broader in others: the U.S. excludes internal use software unless it meets the high threshold of innovation, but carves out customer-facing software entirely and provides the dual function safe harbor, and §41(d)(4)(E) itself excepts software developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research or in a qualifying production process.
7. Documentation and case law
7.1 Court decisions

cells: Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner
T.C. Memo. 2024-113; Tax Court Docket No. 4759-22; filed December 23, 2024 (Judge Greaves).

The Tax Court held that the engineering consulting firm had not shown that the sampled projects involved qualified research, rejecting its assertions of uncertainty and finding that the record did not establish a process of experimentation; the court gave weight to documentation over testimony. Practitioner reports state that the accuracy-related penalties determined by the IRS were sustained. The holding is often characterized in commentary as a failure to identify specific uncertainties at the outset; that framing is commentary rather than a quotation from the opinion. The case also reflects the Tax Court's earlier refusal (order of August 29, 2023) to limit discovery to a handful of example projects. The lesson for CRM claims: generalized statements that "integration was uncertain" will not substitute for contemporaneous, component-level evidence.
Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner
T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (Docket No. 17431-17, filed February 11, 2021), aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), No. 21-3145, decided March 7, 2023.

The taxpayer failed to prove that substantially all (80 percent or more) of its research activities for the business component were elements of a process of experimentation, so none of the claimed expenses were qualified research expenses. The Seventh Circuit affirmed in 2023 while disagreeing with part of the Tax Court's reasoning, including the treatment of direct support and direct supervision activities in the substantially-all fraction. The Seventh Circuit also stressed that shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice and that something more, such as documentation of time spent, is necessary.
Harper v. United States (9th Cir. 2021)

847 F. App'x 408 (9th Cir. 2021), No. 19-55933, filed February 25, 2021 (unpublished memorandum disposition; not precedent except as provided by Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3), reversing No. 3:18-cv-02110-DMS-LL (S.D. Cal. 2019).

The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal and ruled for the taxpayer on the jurisdictional question. The court held that the IRS's substantive, four-year audit specifically directed at the taxpayer's eligibility for the research credit, followed by denial of the claims on the merits, constituted a waiver of the specificity requirement of Treas. Reg. §301.6402-2(b)(1), which requires a refund claim to set forth in detail each ground on which it is made. The waiver rested on the substantive examination and merits denial, not merely on the IRS's acceptance of Form 6765. The case was remanded for further proceedings rather than decided on the merits of the credit.

body.text: 7.2 Scrutiny of refund claims

What is confirmed is the IRS's published screening process: in Chief Counsel memorandum 20214101F (October 15, 2021), the IRS took the position that, to satisfy the specificity requirement of Treas. Reg. §301.6402-2(b)(1), a research credit refund claim must at a minimum identify all business components to which the claim relates for that year; for each business component, identify all research activities performed and name the individuals who performed each activity, as well as the information each individual sought to discover; and provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year. The IRS's Large Business and International division implemented this through interim guidance that gave taxpayers 45 days to perfect a deficient claim during a transition period, which was extended to claims filed through January 9, 2024. Under that guidance, examiners review claims for the required information before considering the merits, and a deficient claim that is not perfected is rejected. The current Instructions for Form 6765 address research credit claims on amended returns.

Form 6765 Section G. The January 2025 revision of Form 6765 added Section G, Business Component Information, which requires qualified research expenses and other information to be reported on a business-component basis. Following IRS announcement IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), Section G was optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026. The Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) state that, for tax years beginning after 2025, Section G will be required, subject to the guidelines in the instructions; practitioner summaries report that qualified small business taxpayers electing the payroll tax credit and taxpayers below specified size thresholds may remain exempt. For CRM claims beginning with 2026 tax years, this means each custom CRM component claimed (for example, "order-synchronization middleware") will need to be identified and supported individually.

Penalties and IRS resources. As to penalties, the Internal Revenue Code provides a 20 percent accuracy-related penalty on underpayments attributable to negligence or a substantial understatement (I.R.C. §6662) and a 20 percent penalty on the excessive amount of a refund claim made without reasonable cause (I.R.C. §6676); accuracy-related penalties were reported as sustained in Phoenix Design Group. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 initially provided the IRS approximately $79.4 billion in supplemental multiyear funding, much of it for enforcement. According to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA), Congress subsequently rescinded $1.4 billion (Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023), $20.2 billion (Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024), another $20.2 billion (Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025) and another $11.7 billion (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026). TIGTA also reported that the IRS workforce fell by approximately 25 percent from February through May 2025. A blanket statement that legislation "increased the IRS workforce" is therefore outdated. Enforcement attention to research credit claims now rests heavily on the reporting requirements described above rather than on expanded headcount.

Specifications stating the intended improvement in function, performance, reliability or quality, distinguishing it from cosmetic or business-process changes.
Technological in nature
Architecture documents and technical notes showing reliance on computer science or engineering principles.
Elimination of uncertainty
Records made at the start of the work identifying what was unknown about capability, method or design, and why vendor documentation, published APIs or certified connectors did not resolve it.
Process of experimentation
Records of the alternatives considered and evaluated, test results including failures, and time or cost records capable of supporting the 80 percent calculation for each business component.
Internal use status (CRM-specific)

A functional map showing which elements are customer- or partner-facing, which are back-office general and administrative, and, for dual function software, any third-party subset and an objective estimate of third-party use (at least 10 percent for the safe harbor).
Refund claim and Form 6765 reporting

For each business component: the research activities, the individuals who performed them, the information sought to be discovered, and qualified wage, supply and contract research expenses, consistent with Chief Counsel memorandum 20214101F and Form 6765 Section G.

11. Conclusion

Customizing a CRM can generate qualifying research under I.R.C. §41, but only for the specific business components, or subsets of components under the shrinking-back rule, where the team faced a real technological uncertainty about capability, method or appropriate design and resolved it through a documented process of experimentation that relied on computer science or engineering principles. That work must meet the 80 percent substantially-all requirement for each business component and must avoid the statutory exclusions for cosmetic changes, post-production activity, adaptation to a particular customer's needs, duplication, and business-process studies. Back-office CRM functionality classed as internal use software must additionally be innovative, involve significant economic risk, and not be commercially available, a demanding combination for work built on a COTS platform. CRM functionality that lets customers or other third parties interact with the taxpayer's system is not internal use software, and dual function CRM software may qualify through a third-party subset or the 25 percent safe harbor. Development costs for qualifying CRM software are research or experimental expenditures under §174A for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. Finally, the case law and IRS procedure reviewed show that U.S. claims succeed or fail on evidence: generalized assertions of uncertainty and reconstructed estimates of experimentation time have not been enough, refund claims must contain the five items of information the IRS requires, and, for tax years beginning after 2025, Form 6765 Section G requires business-component-level reporting.
